cases.title: Albania — children exploited in tourist season; first trafficking convictions since 2021 (US TIP 2025)

patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Nigeria — Kaduna 'Islamic school' raid frees 300+ boys and men

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: UN peacekeeping data, 2025 (SG report A/80/644): Few finalised: e.g. one Togolese officer — repatriation and 60 days' imprisonment; 'pending additional information from the member state'
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended

patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: Bosco Ntaganda (UPC/FPLC, Ituri) — ICC conviction incl. rape and sexual slavery of child soldiers
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC) / Patriotic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (FPLC)
cases.what: On 8 July 2019 ICC Trial Chamber VI found Bosco Ntaganda guilty of 18 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity committed in Ituri in 2002–2003, including rape, sexual slavery and the conscription and use of children under 15; he was the first person convicted of sexual slavery by the ICC. He was sentenced to 30 years on 7 November 2019, confirmed on appeal on 30 March 2021. He had told child soldiers, 'When you're a soldier, you get a woman for free'.

cases.title: Thomas Lubanga (UPC, Ituri) — ICC's first conviction: conscription and use of children
cases.who: Union of Congolese Patriots (UPC/FPLC)
cases.what: On 14 March 2012 the ICC found Thomas Lubanga guilty of enlisting and conscripting children under 15 and using them in hostilities, and sentenced him on 10 July 2012 to 14 years; the verdict was confirmed on 1 December 2014. Sexual violence against girl soldiers was raised at trial but not charged. He was released on 15 March 2020 after serving his sentence.

cases.title: DR Congo — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children by M23, FARDC and armed groups (2024)
cases.who: M23 (68), CODECO (63), FARDC (47), Raia Mutomboki, Nyatura, ADF and others
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 358 girls in the DRC in 2024, by M23 (68), CODECO (63), the Armed Forces of the DRC (47), Raia Mutomboki (33), Nyatura (24) and others, and the abduction of 815 children, by ADF (265), M23 (178) and others. In 2022 it verified sexual violence against 284 children aged 4 to 17, 56 of them by FARDC.

cases.title: Ebola response, North Kivu & Ituri — Independent Commission on SEA by WHO and other responders
cases.who: WHO staff and contractors, Ministry of Health and partner personnel in the 10th Ebola response
cases.what: The Independent Commission appointed by WHO reported on 28 September 2021 that it identified 83 alleged perpetrators, 21 of whom were established with certainty as WHO employees during the response; most were Congolese staff hired temporarily who used their authority to obtain sex, often in exchange for jobs. The review team heard 63 women and 12 men aged 13 to 43; the youngest, a girl selling phone cards in Mangina in April 2019, said a WHO driver raped her. Nine rape allegations were recorded and 29 women and girls became pregnant.

cases.title: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
cases.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cases.what: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.
cases.cover_up: About 750 paternity and child support claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 still pending; claims are referred to troop-contributing countries, most of which have not taken meaningful action

cases.title: MONUC peacekeepers — sexual exploitation of girls in Bunia (OIOS 2004)
cases.who: UN Organization Mission in the DRC (MONUC) military contingents, military observers and civilian staff
cases.what: After media and Congolese women's reports in March and May 2004, OIOS investigated in Bunia from May to September 2004. It found that sexual contact with peacekeepers occurred 'with regularity', usually in exchange for food or small sums of money, and that many cases involved girls under 18, some as young as 13. Of 72 allegations reported to MONUC, many could not be investigated because they were non-specific; six cases were fully substantiated. The findings led to the Secretary-General asking Prince Zeid Ra'ad Al-Hussein of Jordan to prepare the 2005 comprehensive report on SEA by peacekeepers.

cases.title: DR Congo — UN Mapping Report: rape of girls and of child soldiers in military camps by all forces (1993–2003)
cases.who: All parties: FAC (later FARDC), RCD-G, MLC, RCD-K/ML, RCD-N, UPC and PUSIC, FNI and FRPI, FAPC, Mayi-Mayi, ex-FAR/Interahamwe and others
cases.what: The UN human rights office's Mapping Exercise report, published on 1 October 2010, covered the most serious violations in DR Congo between 1993 and 2003. It described 'the apparent systematic use of rape and sexual assault allegedly by all combatant forces' against women and girls, including Hutu refugee children in 1996–97, and the widespread use of child soldiers by all parties, who suffered murder, rape and torture in military camps. It listed 12 parties named by the Secretary-General for recruiting children, among them the national army.

cases.title: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.what: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

cases.title: LRA Makombo massacre and abductions, DR Congo (2009)
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army commanders Lt. Col. Binansio Okumu ('Binany') and 'Obol', reporting to Gen. Dominic Ongwen (per HRW)
cases.what: From 14 to 17 December 2009 Lord's Resistance Army forces attacked at least 10 villages in the remote Makombo area of Haute-Uélé, north-eastern DR Congo, killing at least 321 civilians and abducting 250 others, including at least 80 children. Human Rights Watch, which documented the previously unreported massacre after a field mission in February 2010, said it was carried out by two LRA commanders who reported to Gen. Dominic Ongwen, the senior LRA leader believed to command its forces in Congo and wanted by the International Criminal Court.

cases.title: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
cases.who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
cases.what: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.

cases.title: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
cases.who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
cases.what: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. The UN's 2016 allegations tables (A/71/818) list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA, with 15 child victims.

cases.title: DR Congo — forced labour and sexual exploitation of children at eastern artisanal mines (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Mining bosses, miners, family members, government officials, armed groups
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says mining bosses, other miners, family members, government officials and armed groups force or coerce adults and children into forced labour in artisanal mines in eastern DRC, including through debt bondage, and that most trafficking is internal, including sex trafficking and forced marriage of girls.
cases.cover_up: Traffickers named in the report include government officials; corruption and complicity contributed to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State-backed adoption systems that falsified children's papers
patterns.role_note: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Denmark — state investigation of abuse in special-care institutions 1933–1980 (særforsorgen).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Operation Hamlet — parents sharing abuse of their own children
cases.who: International online network of offenders, many abusing their own children
cases.what: Danish National Police, acting on information from Save the Children about images found online, arrested a man and his wife who had posted images of the abuse of their nine-year-old daughter; from November 2001 the US Customs CyberSmuggling Center coordinated US inquiries with Danish police, INTERPOL and NCMEC. On 9 August 2002 US Customs announced 10 arrests of US citizens, with 10 more suspects arrested in Denmark, Belgium, Germany, England, Switzerland and the Netherlands, and 45 children rescued, 37 of them in the US; in many cases parents were abusing their own children. Fifteen suspects, five of them foreign nationals, were indicted on federal conspiracy charges in the Eastern District of California on 8 August 2002.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Operation Long Arm — 'Bamse' bulletin board (1992)
cases.who: Bamse BBS (Danish bulletin board, ~900 users)
cases.what: US Customs' first major case against internet child abuse material. In late 1992 a US Customs controlled delivery led to a suspect who said he had obtained images from a Europe-based bulletin board; agents found 'Bamse', a Danish bulletin board with child abuse rooms, and two other Danish boards using its images, where users paid a subscription or supplied images of their own. Working with Danish authorities, the operation led to about 35 arrests and convictions in the US. Start year approximate.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Denmark — Appeals Board finds 'systematic illegal behaviour' in Korean adoptions 1970–1989

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)

cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Godhavn Report — Danish state children's homes 1945–1976
cases.who: Danish state-run children's homes incl. Godhavn boys' home
cases.what: The Godhavn Report, published 9 May 2011, examined Godhavn boys' home and 18 other state homes from 1945 to 1976, finding neglect, physical and sexual abuse, and that about 22% of Godhavn residents had been given psychiatric drugs by psychiatrist Ib Ostenfeld. No prosecutions followed. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen apologised to hundreds of victims in 2019.

cases.title: Denmark — state investigation of abuse in special-care institutions 1933–1980 (særforsorgen)
cases.who: Danish state special-care institutions (særforsorgen) for children and adults with intellectual and physical disabilities
cases.what: An investigation ordered by the Danish government in 2020, financed by the Ministry of Social Affairs and the Elderly and carried out by Danmarks Forsorgsmuseum (Svendborg Museum), was published in March 2022. It documented widespread abuse and neglect, including sexual assault, of children, young people and adults placed in state special-care institutions between 1933 and 1980, and found the state did not carry out systematic oversight. About 15,000 people with disabilities were committed. Social affairs minister Pernille Rosenkrantz-Theil gave an official apology on behalf of the state at Horsens on 11 September 2023.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

cases.title: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
cases.who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
cases.what: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Denmark; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Finland — maltreatment in child welfare substitute care 1937–1983

cases.what: A Ministry of Social Affairs and Health study interviewed about 300 people who had been in child welfare substitute care between 1937 and 1983 and found maltreatment and violence in all forms of care. cases.title: Finland — Conservative Laestadian movement (SRK) admits 70–100 child abuse cases mishandled

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 2003: The Gambia: Tourism Offences Act 2003 (child = under 18; hotel operators liable for knowingly allowing child prostitution) 2017: US TIP: traffickers in The Gambia increasingly host child sex tourists in private residences outside the commercial tourist areas, making detection harder
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice
cases.who: Flemish adoption services; intermediaries in Ethiopia and other countries of origin
cases.what: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated 15 February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. Preliminary conclusions found that the true story sometimes differed from the adoption files and that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents. The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

cases.title: The Gambia — child sex tourism on the Senegambia Strip (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Organized networks using European and Gambian travel agencies
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says European tourists, primarily from the UK, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children, and that organized sex-trafficking networks use European and Gambian travel agencies to promote the country as a destination, especially the Senegambia Strip. Women and girls from other West African countries, especially Nigeria, are recruited for tourism jobs and then sexually exploited. The Tourism Offences Act provides life imprisonment for child trafficking by tourists.

flows.title: United Kingdom → The Gambia (travelling offenders)
flows.what: European tourists, primarily from the UK, reportedly travel to The Gambia to exploit children; networks use European and Gambian travel agencies.

cases.title: Rendon-Reyes trafficking organization (Tenancingo)
cases.who: Rendon-Reyes Trafficking Organization, Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
cases.what: From December 2004 to November 2015 the Tenancingo-based Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US, forced them into prostitution and laundered proceeds back to Mexico. In January 2019 five members were sentenced in Brooklyn to between 15 and 25 years; others had pleaded guilty to racketeering and sex trafficking.

cases.title: Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala — gangs exploit girls; North American offenders (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Gangs and criminal organizations; foreign offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP reports say criminal organizations including gangs exploit girls in sex trafficking in urban Honduras and Guatemala, and that men from Canada and the US exploit Honduran children. In El Salvador, foreign tourists sexually exploit children and the rapid growth of tourism has created new risks; an estimated 140,000–200,000 Salvadoran children have a parent abroad or detained. Guatemalan children are exploited in Mexico and the US and in live-streamed abuse.

flows.title: Central America → Mexico → New York (Rendon-Reyes)
flows.what: The Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US for forced prostitution. Origin shown at Honduras for display; the DOJ release says 'Central America' without naming countries.

flows.title: Pennsylvania → El Progreso, Honduras: Fr Joseph Maurizio
flows.what: A Pennsylvania priest abused minors on charity trips to a Honduran orphanage between 2004 and 2009, funded partly through illegal money transfers; convicted 2015.

networks.name: Tenancingo (Tlaxcala) pimping family networks
networks.what: Family-based pimping networks from Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, that recruited Mexican and Central American women and girls by deception and forced them into prostitution in New York and other US cities. Several were prosecuted in Brooklyn (Carreto family, 2005–2008; Rendon-Reyes organization, 2019).

patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls.
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.title: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024

cases.what: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. cases.who: Da'esh; HPG/PKK

cases.title: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls
cases.who: Islamic State (ISIS/Da'esh)
cases.what: ISIS attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis in an organised manner to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush prison, the Galaxy wedding hall) and Baaj, and women and girls onward to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found in June 2016 ('They came to destroy') that ISIS committed genocide; women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. cases.who: Security and military officials (alleged, per an international organization); criminal gangs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says women and girls in IDP camps whose relatives have alleged ISIS ties may face sexual exploitation and sex trafficking by security and military officials, and that some officials allegedly exploit such families, including children, in exchange for documents. Criminal gangs reportedly exploit Syrian women and girls at pilgrimage sites, and Yezidi survivors remain at risk of re-trafficking.
cases.cover_up: An international organization reported in 2024 that officials coerce family members of detained children into sex acts in exchange for security clearances or civil documents; the government reported no action on official complicity.

flows.what: Captives were moved in buses and trucks to holding sites in Tal Afar and Mosul, then women and girls were transferred to Raqqa and sold.

networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 6,541 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

cases.title: Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan — girls lured to cities; children in institutions (US TIP 2025)

In Uzbekistan, children in institutions are vulnerable to sex trafficking.

cases.who: Nigerian trafficking networks via Libya
cases.what: In July 2017 the International Organization for Migration said perhaps 80 per cent of Nigerian migrant women and girls arriving by sea in Italy could be sex-trafficking victims, and that its Italy office had seen an almost 600 per cent rise in potential victims over three years. IOM indicators included age (most victims 13–24) and being 'controlled' by other migrants. Thomson Reuters Foundation later cited IOM data that Nigerian female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016.

cases.title: Libya — sex trafficking of sub-Saharan girls in southern brothels; abuse of transiting children (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Commercial sex rings; armed groups; officials
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says commercial sex rings subject sub-Saharan women and girls to sex trafficking in brothels, particularly in Ubari, Sabha and Murzuq, and that Nigerian women and girls are at increased risk. It cites an international organization finding that 77 per cent of children and youth transiting Libya experienced indicators of exploitation amounting to trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Observers report systemic official complicity, including Libyan Coast Guard, immigration and security officials; the government has never reported prosecuting or convicting anyone for sex or labour trafficking.

cases.title: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.what: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner took a 14-year-old girl and her 12-year-old brother in the night from their mother's home in upstate New York and moved them through several states to Mexico, where the girl was returned to the adult man the group had 'married' her to religiously at 13. The mother had fled the group's Guatemala compound in November 2018 and been granted sole custody. Both children were recovered in Mexico after three weeks. A federal jury convicted the two men in November 2021, and on 31 March 2022 each was sentenced to 12 years. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.

cases.title: Jean Succar Kuri — Cancún child sexual exploitation ring
cases.who: Jean Succar Kuri (hotelier); associates named in Lydia Cacho's reporting
cases.what: Cancún hotel businessman Succar Kuri was detained in the United States (reported as Los Angeles/Arizona) in 2004 at the request of Mexico's federal prosecutors and Interpol, after complaints by several girls, and was later returned to Mexico. In 2011 a federal district court convicted him and sentenced him to 13 years; on appeal by both sides a Cancún appeals court raised the sentence to 112 years, which was upheld. In 2023 a federal circuit court annulled the 112-year sentence over procedural flaws and ordered a new ruling on sexual abuse and child pornography offences against seven minors, which reduced his term. He died in Cancún on 14 June 2024 while still serving his sentence. Journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' described him as the head of a child-exploitation network and linked him to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Governor Mario Marín.
cases.cover_up: See the related record on journalist Lydia Cacho's 2005 arrest arranged after her book exposed the ring.

cases.title: Carreto family — Tenancingo to New York trafficking
cases.who: Carreto family pimping network based in Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
cases.what: From 1991 to 2004 the Carreto family, based in San Miguel de Tenancingo, Tlaxcala, recruited young, poor women and girls in Mexico by deception and forced them into prostitution in brothels in Queens and Brooklyn, using rape, threats and forced abortion. Josue and Gerardo Flores Carreto were sentenced to 50 years each in April 2006 and Daniel Perez Alonso to 25 years. Their mother Consuelo Carreto Valencia was extradited in January 2007 and pleaded guilty to sex trafficking on 22 July 2008.

cases.title: Rendon-Reyes trafficking organization (Tenancingo)
cases.who: Rendon-Reyes Trafficking Organization, Tenancingo, Tlaxcala
cases.what: From December 2004 to November 2015 the Tenancingo-based Rendon-Reyes organization smuggled women and girls from Mexico and Central America into the US, forced them into prostitution and laundered proceeds back to Mexico. In January 2019 five members were sentenced in Brooklyn to between 15 and 25 years; others had pleaded guilty to racketeering and sex trafficking.

cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month; she was released on parole in 2023. US ICE supported the investigation.
cases.cover_up: At hearings she threatened to reveal the names of politicians and powerful men she said were clients (her claim, unverified).

cases.title: Costa Rica — Fr Mauricio Víquez, convicted after fleeing to Mexico
cases.who: Archdiocese of San José; Episcopal Conference of Costa Rica
cases.what: Víquez, a former church spokesman on family issues, fled Costa Rica in 2018 when accusations surfaced, going via Panama to San Nicolás de los Garza, Mexico, where he was caught; he was extradited in 2021. The church expelled him from the clergy in 2019. In March 2022 he was sentenced to 20 years (6 for sexual abuse, 14 for rape) for abusing an 11-year-old boy in his parish in 2002–2003. In August 2022 a civil court ordered the archbishop and two church entities to pay about US$100,000 in damages.
cases.cover_up: A San José civil court ordered Archbishop José Rafael Quirós, the Episcopal Conference and the church's property entity to pay 65 million colones; the victims' lawyer said the church knew from 2002 and did nothing. Three other complaints were declared time-barred.

cases.title: NXIVM — Keith Raniere convicted (including sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old)
cases.who: NXIVM (self-help group run as a cult)
cases.what: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted NXIVM leader Keith Raniere in June 2019 of racketeering, racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking, attempted sex trafficking, forced labour conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy. Prosecutors proved as racketeering acts that at 45 he sexually exploited a 15-year-old girl and photographed the abuse. On 27 October 2020 he was sentenced to 120 years and fined $1.75 million.

cases.title: La Luz del Mundo — leader Naasón Joaquín García convicted
cases.who: La Luz del Mundo church (HQ Guadalajara, Mexico)
cases.what: Naasón Joaquín García, leader of La Luz del Mundo, was arrested at Los Angeles International Airport on 3 June 2019 on charges brought by the California Attorney General including forcible rape of a minor, production of child pornography and human trafficking. On 3 June 2022, days before trial, he pleaded guilty to three counts involving minors (two of forcible oral copulation and one lewd act on a 15-year-old), and on 8 June 2022 was sentenced to more than 16 years in prison. Co-defendant Alondra Ocampo pleaded guilty to four counts in 2020. In October 2023 a federal grand jury indicted him for producing and possessing child pornography involving a 16-year-old follower.

cases.title: Marcial Maciel and the Legion of Christ — 2019 internal report
cases.who: Legion of Christ (Legionaries); founder Marcial Maciel
cases.what: For decades until 2006 the Vatican dismissed accusations by seminarians that founder Marcial Maciel had abused them. In 2006 it ordered him to retire to a life of 'prayer and penitence', and on 1 May 2010, after an apostolic visitation, it said his acts were 'true crimes'. The Legion's own report, released on 21 December 2019, found that 175 minors were abused by 33 of its priests between 1941 and 2019; at least 60 of them by Maciel. It said 111 of the 175 were victims of Maciel or of his victims, and that 14 of the 33 abusive priests had themselves been abused within the order.
cases.cover_up: Letters to the Vatican in 1976, 1978 and 1989 and formal charges in 1998 produced no action; Vatican in 2010 said the Legion had shielded Maciel; Maciel never laicised or tried

cases.title: Mexico — bishops say 152 priests removed in nine years
cases.who: Mexican Episcopal Conference (CEM)
cases.what: On 10 February 2019 Archbishop Rogelio Cabrera of Monterrey, president of the Mexican Episcopal Conference, said 152 priests had been removed from ministry in the previous nine years after being found guilty of sexually abusing minors, some of whom were jailed. He said there was no exact figure for victims.
cases.cover_up: The CEM president said there was no national count of victims because 'each bishop handles these problems' and no central record exists.

cases.title: Mexican bishops' conference — 426 priests investigated
cases.who: Conferencia del Episcopado Mexicano
cases.what: On 14 January 2020 the Mexican Episcopal Conference said it was investigating 426 priests over the previous ten years: 271 cases of abuse of minors in church settings and 155 other proceedings. It said 217 priests had been removed from their duties. El Universal reported in February 2020 that prosecutors had opened 156 investigations into such sexual offences by religious figures from 2009 to 2019, but four prosecutors' offices recorded only six sentences.
cases.cover_up: El Universal reported only six convictions out of 156 alleged abuse cases involving minors, 2009–2019

cases.title: La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora
cases.who: La Gran Familia shelter, founded 1947 by Rosa del Carmen Verduzco ('Mamá Rosa')
cases.what: On 15 July 2014 the PGR's organised-crime unit (SEIDO) raided the shelter and freed 432 children and 138 adults living in squalid conditions; the PGR said some had suffered sexual abuse, and residents reported rape, being held for years, food deprivation and forced begging. The PGR ruled out charging the 79-year-old founder because of age and mental decline; six others faced charges from unlawful imprisonment to organised crime. The PGR also investigated claims that the shelter in effect bought children through notarised parental waivers. Verduzco died in 2018.
cases.cover_up: More than 40 complaints from parents had been filed with Michoacán's DIF and the federal Attorney General's Office (PGR) before the raid.

cases.title: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters
cases.who: Iglesia Cristiana Restaurada (Restored Christian Church) shelters; Mexico City Attorney General's Office (PGJDF), which placed children there
cases.what: Children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the private Casitas del Sur shelter, run by a church group, went missing. In October 2010 Mexico's federal Attorney General offered rewards for information on 14 children who disappeared in February 2009 from the Casitas del Sur shelter in Mexico City and from related homes in Nuevo Laredo and Quintana Roo, and about 5 million pesos for three people sought in the case, saying the children may have been taken by child traffickers. Earlier sources not re-checked for this map also cite the removal of 126 children by police and human rights staff on 29 January 2009 and obstruction charges against seven staff (not re-checked for this map).
cases.cover_up: A Mexico City legislator accused officials of the District Attorney's office of negligence and complicity, saying they warned the shelter of searches so children could be moved.

cases.title: Fr Nicolás Aguilar Rivera — Puebla diocese priest in Los Angeles
cases.who: Archdiocese of Los Angeles; Diocese of Tehuacán (Mexico)
cases.what: A visiting Mexican priest was assigned to two Los Angeles parishes in 1987. A 1988 police report says he abused 26 grade-school children between March 1987 and January 1988, many recruited as altar servers. A parent reported abuse to a pastor on 8 January 1988; he was removed the next day, charged with 19 felony counts of lewd acts on a child, but fled to Mexico before arrest. As of 2004 the case remained open.
cases.cover_up: Plaintiffs' attorneys produced a 1988 letter from the Bishop of Tehuacán saying he had warned Cardinal Mahony in 1987 about the priest; the archdiocese denied receiving the warning. The priest fled to Mexico after being relieved of duties and was never arrested.

cases.title: Lydia Cacho's arrest — Puebla governor and businessman protected exploitation ring
cases.who: Mario Marín (Governor of Puebla); Kamel Nacif Borge (businessman)
cases.what: After journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' (2005) linked Cancún businessman Jean Succar Kuri's child-exploitation network to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Puebla governor Mario Marín, Cacho was arrested in 2005 and says she was tortured. Arrest warrants for torture were issued against Marín and Nacif; Marín was arrested in Acapulco in February 2021, and Nacif was detained in Lebanon in May 2021 and later released there. Marín was moved to house arrest in August 2024, returned to prison in April 2025, and in July 2026 was again granted house arrest on health and age grounds while his trial for alleged torture of Cacho continues. Neither has been convicted; both are accused of torture, not of the abuse itself.
cases.cover_up: Intimidation of a journalist: after Cacho exposed the Cancún ring, Puebla police arrested her in Cancún and drove her about 900 miles to Puebla. Leaked calls (La Jornada, 14 Feb 2006) recorded Nacif and Marín discussing jailing her as a favour and having her abused in jail. Mexico's Supreme Court ruled 6–4 on 29 Nov 2007 that Marín had no case to answer.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 1 documented adoption flows into New Zealand on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2005: New Zealand Crimes Amendment Act 2005 criminalises sexual conduct with children abroad by citizens and residents
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding; Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Dilworth School — Anglican boarding school, Auckland
cases.who: Dilworth Trust (Anglican-linked school for boys from disadvantaged families)
cases.what: Police arrested and charged six men on 14 September 2020 over offences at Dilworth alleged to date from the 1970s to the early 2000s. An independent inquiry led by Dame Silvia Cartwright and Frances Joychild KC, released on 18 September 2023 and covering 1950 to the present, found that sexual abuse was committed consistently from the mid-1950s to the end of 2005: 126 of 171 former students who gave information reported being sexually abused, and the inquiry knew of 49 more. Police estimated 233 student victims. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care also examined Dilworth.
cases.cover_up: The independent inquiry concluded that ongoing silence about the abuse was 'the primary reason for the damage' to former students.

cases.title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
cases.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
cases.what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. The main administrator in Thailand and a second administrator in Adelaide, Australia, were arrested in January 2018. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

cases.title: Matthew Falder — dark web 'hurtcore' blackmailer
cases.who: Individual offender posting on hurtcore dark web sites
cases.what: A Cambridge-educated Birmingham university researcher posed online as a depressed female artist to lure victims, some as young as 14, into sending images, then blackmailed them into sending increasingly degrading material, which he shared on dark web 'hurtcore' sites. The NCA estimated more than 50 victims between 2009 and 2017. A taskforce of the NCA, GCHQ, US Homeland Security Investigations, the Australian Federal Police and Europol, with police in Israel and Slovenia, identified him after four years; he was arrested in June 2017. He admitted 137 of 188 charges and was jailed for 32 years in February 2018, thought to be the first UK prosecution related to hurtcore material; in October 2018 the Court of Appeal reduced the sentence to 25 years.
cases.cover_up: The NCA said technology companies' limited cooperation may have delayed identifying victims.

cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Marist Brothers and priests — New Zealand convictions
cases.who: Marist Brothers; Society of Mary
cases.what: A 2018 Otago Daily Times report listed nine Marist Brothers convicted of crimes against boys in New Zealand, including two at Hato Paora College. Marist priest Alan Woodcock was extradited from England and convicted in 2004 of 21 offences (1978–1987). Brother Kevin Healy was convicted in 2020. The church admitted in 2022 that 14% of its diocesan clergy had been accused since 1950.

cases.title: Fiji — transferred clergy and Julian Fox
cases.who: Salesians; Catholic Church in Fiji
cases.what: Salesian priest Julian Fox was moved to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating abuse allegations; he was jailed in Australia in 2015. The Catholic Church in Fiji knew of the allegations nine years before he was charged. In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.
cases.cover_up: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged

cases.title: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report
cases.who: State social welfare, disability, mental health, education, law-enforcement and faith-based care settings
cases.what: The final report, made public on 24 July 2024, found abuse was rife in state and faith-based care and that sexual abuse was commonplace, with abusers grooming people in care. It estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 were abused; Māori were more likely to be abused. Commissioners Coral Shaw, Andrew Erueti and Paul Gibson made 138 recommendations, including a specialist investigation unit and an independent Care Safe Agency, and called it 'a national disgrace'.
cases.cover_up: Commissioners found the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and neglect, and that by 2024 there had been very little progress on the redress system they recommended in 2021.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: New Zealand — Confidential Listening and Assistance Service final report, 'Some memories never fade' (2015)
cases.who: New Zealand state care: residential special education, health and welfare institutions
cases.what: The New Zealand Government set up the Confidential Listening and Assistance Service, chaired by Judge Carolyn Henwood, in 2008 to hear people who had been abused or neglected in state care before 1992. It heard 1,103 participants and finished in June 2015; its final report, 'Some memories never fade', was released under the Official Information Act in August 2015. The panel described 'an alarming amount of abuse and neglect, with extreme levels of violence', including physical, sexual, emotional and verbal abuse, across the 50 years before 1992, and said much of it was preventable with better oversight.

cases.title: Royal Commission into Abuse in Care — Catholic institutions
cases.who: Catholic Church in Aotearoa New Zealand; St John of God Brothers at Marylands School
cases.what: The Royal Commission's final report, Whanaketia, published 24 July 2024, found about 200,000 people were abused in state and faith-based care from 1950 to 2019. It found Catholic responses inadequate, noting a 2020 church briefing that 14% of clergy were accused over 1950–1999, and singled out Marylands School in Christchurch for some of the highest levels of sexual abuse. It found abusers were transferred to other ministries and recommended an inquiry into priests sent to Papua New Guinea.
cases.cover_up: Church relied on psychiatrists' opinions to transfer abusers to other ministries where they reoffended; commission recommended investigating priests transferred to Papua New Guinea

cases.title: Marylands School and Hebron Trust — St John of God Brothers
cases.who: Brothers Hospitallers of St John of God
cases.what: Marylands, a Christchurch residential school for boys with learning disabilities run by the St John of God Brothers, and the order's later Hebron Trust were described by survivors to the Royal Commission as 'hell on earth'. Its August 2023 report found widespread sexual and physical abuse: more than one in five of the 537 boys who attended Marylands reported abuse between 1955 and 1984, and 21 of the 37 Brothers who served at Marylands and in Christchurch faced abuse allegations. At Hebron Trust youths were abused by Brother Bernard McGrath, who has been convicted of more than 100 offences in New Zealand and Australia.
cases.cover_up: Brother Bernard McGrath was transferred to Australia after 1977 allegations and later put in charge of Hebron Trust; victims sometimes required to sign non-disclosure agreements

cases.title: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
cases.who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
cases.what: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.
cases.cover_up: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.

cases.title: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
cases.who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
cases.what: Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic and painful paraldehyde injections used as punishment, and evidence was given of children being raped and sexually abused by staff and adult patients. In 2019 the UN Committee Against Torture found New Zealand had breached the Convention by failing to investigate properly; police opened a new investigation in 2020. Psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found many of the children were tortured, and on 18 Dec 2024 the government announced NZ$150,000 redress per survivor and a new Crown apology explicitly acknowledging torture.
cases.cover_up: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.

cases.title: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
cases.who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
cases.what: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

cases.title: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
cases.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
cases.what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

cases.title: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
cases.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
cases.what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

cases.title: Project COMPASS against 'The Com' network
cases.who: The Com (decentralised online network incl. 764, CVLT)
cases.what: Coordinated by Europol's European Counter Terrorism Centre with EU states, Norway, Switzerland, the UK, US, Canada, Australia and New Zealand (28 countries). Since January 2025 it has contributed to 30 arrests, 179 identified or partially identified perpetrators, 62 identified or partially identified victims and 4 victims safeguarded. The FBI warned the public about The Com on 23 July 2025.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: CVLT — neo-Nazi child exploitation group leaders arrested
cases.who: CVLT (part of 'The Com')
cases.what: On 30 January 2025 US HSI arrested two men for participating in CVLT, which groomed and coerced at least 16 minors worldwide into producing abuse material and self-harm imagery. Europol said earlier-arrested members included one in French custody since 2022 and one serving a 50-year US sentence. Europol describes these communities as part of 'The Com'.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

flows.title: Seoul → New Zealand
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to New Zealand; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: UK → New Zealand child migrants
flows.what: New Zealand's Social Development Minister said in November 2009 that 549 British child migrants arrived between 1948 and 1954 and that most were placed in foster care rather than institutions; IICSA lists New Zealand among the destinations of British child migration.

flows.title: New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath
flows.what: After allegations surfaced in 1977, the St John of God order transferred McGrath to Australia, where he later faced 252 charges; he was also convicted in New Zealand.

flows.title: New Zealand → Papua New Guinea: priests sent after allegations
flows.what: New Zealand's Royal Commission into Abuse in Care (2024) found the church transferred abusers to other ministries and recommended an investigation into Catholic priests sent to Papua New Guinea after abuse allegations. Numbers not stated.

flows.title: Australia / New Zealand → Fiji: transferred clergy
flows.what: 1News reported in July 2020 that some of about 1,300 alleged clergy child abuse cases in Fiji involved clergy from Australia and New Zealand, and a survivor advocate said Fiji was a common destination for transferred clergy.

flows.title: New Zealand → Sydney (Frank Houston)
flows.what: Frank Houston led the Assemblies of God in New Zealand from 1965 to 1977, abusing boys there, then moved to Sydney; Assemblies of God investigations found six further credible allegations in Australia and New Zealand. Origin is a country centroid.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: The Com
networks.what: Transnational network of online groups (incl. 764, CVLT) involved in sextortion, child sexual exploitation, swatting and other crimes; FBI public warning 23 July 2025; Europol Project COMPASS since 2025. Start year approximate.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Marist Brothers
networks.what: Teaching order founded in France. Listed 154 members accused in Australia (1980–2015); nine Brothers convicted in New Zealand; apologised for systemic abuse at Scottish schools; acknowledged at least 14 victims of one Brother in Chile; complaints against 12 teachers at Barcelona schools.

networks.name: Salesians of Don Bosco
networks.what: Order present in more than 130 countries. Documented cases include Boys' Town Sydney, the Don Rua juvenate in the Netherlands, US schools, Julian Fox (moved from Australia to Fiji in 1999), and Vatican sanctions on Salesian Bishop Belo of Timor-Leste.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2014: Puerto Rico — Arecibo diocese and island-wide justice department probe.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: Puerto Rico — Arecibo priests defrocked; island-wide probe
cases.who: Diocese of Arecibo; at least four Puerto Rican dioceses
cases.what: In early 2014, after reports in El Nuevo Día, Bishop Daniel Fernández disclosed that since 2011 he had expelled six priests accused of sexual abuse in the Arecibo diocese. Local prosecutors said at least 11 other priests on the island were under investigation, and the Justice Secretary said at least four dioceses were being investigated. U.S. Homeland Security Investigations requested information.
cases.cover_up: Prosecutor Yolanda Pitino said the diocese's information was insufficient and it had not answered requests for more; Justice Secretary César Miranda warned he might charge church officials suspected of withholding information.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2007: suspension: Ireland's Adoption Board suspends adoptions from Ethiopia and Rwanda (10 October)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.
