patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: UN peacekeeping data, 2025 (SG report A/80/644): Few finalised: e.g. one Togolese officer — repatriation and 60 days' imprisonment; 'pending additional information from the member state'
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: South Sudan — 'sex for aid' allegations against aid workers, Malakal UN Protection of Civilians site.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: Almost no reports reach the international systems
patterns.role_note: NCMEC 2025: 863 reports for South Sudan
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: South Sudan — sexual violence against girls by SSPDF and other forces (UN verified)
cases.who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces (SSPDF), SPLM/A-IO factions, police
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls, as young as 7, in South Sudan in 2022, 74 of them by the South Sudan People's Defence Forces, plus SPLM/A-IO Kit-Gwang (10), SPLM/A-IO (4) and the National Police Service (2). In 2024 it verified sexual violence against 7 girls, 5 by the SSPDF.

cases.title: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
cases.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cases.what: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.

cases.title: South Sudan — UN Commission finds rape, abduction and sexual slavery of women and girls by armed forces and groups (2022)
cases.who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces, opposition forces and armed groups; intercommunal militias
cases.what: The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan presented a report on conflict-related sexual violence to the Human Rights Council on 18 March 2022. It found that parties to the conflict used rape of women and girls as a weapon of terror and political repression, and that abductions of women and girls for forced marriage and sexual slavery had increased in Jonglei, the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, Warrap and Lakes. It noted that a military court in Yei had convicted SSPDF soldiers of rape in late 2020 but victims had not been paid court-ordered compensation.
cases.cover_up: Commission described impunity for armed forces in Western Equatoria; court-ordered compensation to victims in Yei unpaid

cases.title: South Sudan — 'sex for aid' allegations against aid workers, Malakal UN Protection of Civilians site
cases.who: Staff named from IOM, MSF, WFP, World Vision and others in a UN-run camp
cases.what: A September 2022 investigation by The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022 aid workers in the UN-run Malakal Protection of Civilians site exploited displaced women and girls, including 'sex for aid'; women and girls reported being raped and becoming pregnant. Staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named.

flows.title: Northern Uganda → South Sudan: LRA abducted children
flows.what: LRA bases in southern Sudan held abducted Ugandan children.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 6,478 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2011: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 1996: Thailand: an act passed in 1996 prohibits sex with a person under 18 in a prostitution establishment regardless of consent 2008: Thailand: Anti-Human Trafficking Act B.E. 2551 (2008) 2017: Thailand denied entry to 74 known foreign sex offenders in 2017
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Patong, Phuket — foreign bar owner sentenced to 1,073 years after raid freed six minors (2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Swiss bar owner jailed 16 years for abusing more than 80 boys in Pattaya and northern Thailand
cases.who: Unnamed Swiss national (72, from Lucerne) who ran a bar in Pattaya
cases.what: A Swiss man previously convicted of abusing children in Fribourg (1980) and Valais (1991) returned to Thailand in 1996 and, mainly in 2002–2013, abused more than 80 boys in Pattaya, where he ran a bar with a hotel room frequented by Europeans, and in Nong Hoi in the north; he also forced boys to perform acts with European clients. Charged in Fribourg with human trafficking, encouraging prostitution, sexual acts with children and abuse material, he was sentenced by a Swiss court on 1 March 2018 to 16 years.

cases.title: Operation Blackwrist — Thai boys abused for Tor sites
cases.who: Tor site administrators in Thailand and Australia
cases.what: INTERPOL launched Operation Blackwrist in 2017 after finding, during routine dark web monitoring, material showing the abuse of 11 boys under 13, published weekly on a subscription website with nearly 63,000 users. Bulgaria's cybercrime police, supported by Europol, took down the servers; US HSI, New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs, NCMEC and Australian police assisted. In June 2018 a Thai court sentenced the Thai administrator to 146 years, and an associate received 36 years; on 17 May 2019 the Australian administrator was sentenced to 40 years and three months, the longest sentence ever imposed in Australia for child sex offences. INTERPOL said 50 children had been removed from harm and 9 offenders arrested in Thailand, Australia and the United States.

cases.title: Patong, Phuket — foreign bar owner sentenced to 1,073 years after raid freed six minors (2024)
cases.who: Illegal bar on Bangla Road
cases.what: A 2023 raid on an illegal bar on Bangla Road, Patong, rescued six victims of child sexual exploitation under 18. On 19 July 2024 the Phuket Provincial Court sentenced seven defendants, Thai and foreign; the prime defendant, a foreign owner, received a total of 1,073 years. Five senior Patong police were transferred after the raid. The 2025 US TIP report says children from Thailand, Burma, Cambodia and Laos are increasingly sex-trafficked in brothels, bars, karaoke lounges and hotels.
cases.cover_up: Five senior Patong police officers were transferred after the raid; the foreign owner initially fled to a neighbouring country.

cases.title: Mark Frost — 13 life terms for abuse of boys in Thailand and the UK (2017)
cases.who: Mark Frost (also known as Andrew Tracey), former teacher and scout leader
cases.what: Frost, who had held positions of trust in UK schools and scouting and first admitted an offence in 1992, abused boys from poor families in Thailand in 2011–2013, including streaming abuse by webcam to another European man. In February 2017 he was sentenced to 13 terms of life imprisonment after pleading guilty to 45 offences against boys in the UK and Thailand. The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse cited the case as one of only about eight successful UK prosecutions since 1997 for offences committed abroad. Eight Thai boys secured civil compensation in 2018.

cases.title: Thailand — 'Baby 101' surrogate baby-breeding operation
cases.who: Baby 101 company
cases.what: In February 2011 Thai police freed 14 Vietnamese women, half of them pregnant, held in two Bangkok houses with passports confiscated by a company called Baby 101 that took orders from childless couples for newborns. A Taiwanese woman said to run the operation was charged with human trafficking; four said they had been tricked, and the health minister said some appeared to have been raped.

cases.title: ECPAT 'Offenders on the Move' — Global Study on Sexual Exploitation of Children in Travel and Tourism (2016)
cases.who: ECPAT International and partners (High-Level Task Force chaired by Najat Maalla M'jid)
cases.what: Published 12 May 2016 after two years' work, the study found sexual exploitation of children in travel and tourism had grown despite 20 years of effort, as international arrivals rose from 527 million to 1.135 billion a year. It found there is no typical offender: most are domestic or regional travellers and 'situational' offenders rather than Western paedophiles; the internet has opened new pathways; and conviction rates are alarmingly low. It identified the US and Canada as source countries for offenders and Europe as a source, with exploitation rising in Central and Eastern Europe.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked

patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen.
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: Uganda — European Adoption Consultants bribery scheme; judges sanctioned
cases.who: European Adoption Consultants (Ohio, defunct); Ugandan lawyers and judges
cases.what: Between 2013 and 2016 the Ohio agency European Adoption Consultants arranged the adoption of more than 30 Ugandan children by US families; families were promised their children would attend school in Kampala but they were taken to an unlicensed home. On 14 August 2020 a federal indictment charged two EAC employees and Ugandan lawyer Dorah Mirembe (allegations; presumed innocent); an earlier employee, Robin Longoria, pleaded guilty in August 2019 to bribing Ugandan officials. On 17–18 August 2020 the US State Department sanctioned Ugandan judges Moses Mukiibi and Wilson Musalu Musene and lawyers Mirembe and Patrick Ecobu.
cases.cover_up: Bribes were paid to Ugandan judges and other officials to secure adoption orders.

cases.title: Kenya — child sex trafficking in Kilifi/Kwale villas; Karamoja girls to Nairobi (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Family members, taxi drivers, recruiters; foreign and local offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report cites a 2023 NGO study estimating that more than 2,000 children were exploited in child sex trafficking in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and vacation homes rather than hotels. It also reports cross-border rings moving women and underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and truck drivers, miners and Lake Victoria fishermen exploiting children.
cases.cover_up: The report notes ongoing concerns of official complicity with no reported action against complicit officials.

cases.title: Uganda — over 500 unlicensed children's homes outside state oversight
cases.who: Uganda Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development; unlicensed children's homes, many foreign-funded
cases.what: Uganda's Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development says only 185 children's homes are fully licensed (holding 9,486 children) and that more than 500 unlicensed institutions operate without oversight, exposing children to neglect, exploitation and abuse. The ministry's principal probation officer said many children in homes are not orphans, and that some are survivors of trafficking or sexual abuse. The government has closed unregistered homes, including Hope Center Uganda (American board) after a raid that found children in poor conditions.

cases.title: AMISOM bases, Mogadishu — rape and sexual exploitation (HRW 2014)
cases.who: African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) Ugandan and Burundian contingents
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's report of 8 September 2014, based on 50 interviews including 21 survivors, documented 10 incidents of sexual abuse, including rape and sexual assault, and 14 cases of sexual exploitation by African Union (AMISOM) soldiers, mainly Ugandan personnel at and around AMISOM's headquarters and Burundian personnel at their base in Mogadishu. Four rape cases and one sexual assault involved girls under 18; the youngest was a 12-year-old allegedly raped by a Ugandan soldier near Baidoa in May 2013. Many victims had gone to the bases to seek medicine or aid, including a woman seeking medicine for her sick baby, and interpreters facilitated soldiers' access; some women and girls were compelled into sex in exchange for money, food and medicine.

cases.title: Uganda — Karamojong children sold at border markets (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers including community 'elders'
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says NGOs estimate the majority of child sex-trafficking victims in Uganda are ethnically Karamojong, especially from Napak district. Traffickers, sometimes community 'elders', force children to meet them at international borders, where markets are organized to sell children into domestic servitude or sex trafficking. Women, girls and boys are exploited in Kampala brothels, bars and homes.

networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Melbourne → Samoa: Salesian priest (alleged).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.
